claim: Transcription factors are crucial regulators of gene expression.
source: Transcription factors are crucial regulators of gene expression.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about the role of transcription factors.

claim: Accurate quantitative definition of transcription factor DNA binding preferences is critical to understanding their biological function.
source: Accurate quantitative definition of their intrinsic DNA binding preferences is critical to understanding their biological function.
evidence: This represents a general principle in the field based on established understanding.

claim: High-throughput in vitro technology has been used to probe the DNA binding specificity of hundreds of eukaryotic transcription factors.
source: High-throughput in vitro technology has recently been used to deeply probe the DNA binding specificity of hundreds of eukaryotic transcription factors, yet algorithms for analyzing such data have not yet fully matured.
evidence: This statement refers to the current state of the field and available technology.

claim: Algorithms for analyzing high-throughput in vitro protein-DNA binding data have not yet fully matured.
source: High-throughput in vitro technology has recently been used to deeply probe the DNA binding specificity of hundreds of eukaryotic transcription factors, yet algorithms for analyzing such data have not yet fully matured.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of computational methods in the field.

claim: FeatureREDUCE is a general framework for building sequence-to-affinity models based on a biophysically interpretable model of protein-DNA interaction.
source: Here, we present a general framework (FeatureREDUCE) for building sequence-to-affinity models based on a biophysically interpretable and extensible model of protein-DNA interaction that can account for dependencies between nucleotides within the binding interface or multiple modes of binding.
evidence: This describes the nature and capabilities of the FeatureREDUCE framework presented in the manuscript.

claim: FeatureREDUCE can account for dependencies between nucleotides within the binding interface.
source: Here, we present a general framework (FeatureREDUCE) for building sequence-to-affinity models based on a biophysically interpretable and extensible model of protein-DNA interaction that can account for dependencies between nucleotides within the binding interface or multiple modes of binding.
evidence: This is a stated capability of the FeatureREDUCE method.

claim: FeatureREDUCE can account for multiple modes of binding.
source: Here, we present a general framework (FeatureREDUCE) for building sequence-to-affinity models based on a biophysically interpretable and extensible model of protein-DNA interaction that can account for dependencies between nucleotides within the binding interface or multiple modes of binding.
evidence: This is a stated capability of the FeatureREDUCE method.

claim: FeatureREDUCE uses robust regression when training on PBM data.
source: When training on protein binding microarray (PBM) data, we use robust regression and modeling of technology-specific biases to infer specificity models of unprecedented accuracy and precision.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in FeatureREDUCE.

claim: FeatureREDUCE models technology-specific biases when training on PBM data.
source: When training on protein binding microarray (PBM) data, we use robust regression and modeling of technology-specific biases to infer specificity models of unprecedented accuracy and precision.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in FeatureREDUCE.

claim: FeatureREDUCE infers specificity models of unprecedented accuracy and precision.
source: When training on protein binding microarray (PBM) data, we use robust regression and modeling of technology-specific biases to infer specificity models of unprecedented accuracy and precision.
evidence: This is a claim about the performance of FeatureREDUCE supported by validation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transcription factors play a central role in the regulation of gene expression.
source: Transcription factors (TFs) play a central role in the regulation of gene expression.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about transcription factors.

claim: Understanding in vivo DNA binding preferences of transcription factors is necessary to understand and predict gene regulatory circuitry behavior.
source: To be able to understand and predict the behavior of the gene regulatory circuitry in any given organism, we need to know the in vivo DNA binding preferences of the TFs that its genome encodes.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the role of TFs in gene regulation.

claim: A number of high-throughput in vitro technologies have been introduced in recent years to measure TF DNA binding preferences.
source: In recent years, a number of high-throughput in vitro technologies have been introduced that can provide such information (Berger and Bulyk, 2009; Warren et al., 2006; Maerkl and Quake, 2007; Zhao et al., 2009; Slattery et al., 2011; Berger et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: The volume of data generated using high-throughput assays dwarfs that of traditional measurements of protein-DNA interaction strength.
source: However, while the volume of the data generated using these assays dwarfs that of more traditional measurements of protein-DNA interaction strength, the available computational methodology for analyzing them has not fully matured (Weirauch, 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of data volumes between different measurement approaches.

claim: The available computational methodology for analyzing high-throughput protein-DNA binding data has not fully matured.
source: However, while the volume of the data generated using these assays dwarfs that of more traditional measurements of protein-DNA interaction strength, the available computational methodology for analyzing them has not fully matured (Weirauch, 2013).
evidence: This assessment is supported by a citation to Weirauch 2013.

claim: The number of base pairs that constitute the DNA footprint depends strongly on the three-dimensional structure of the DNA-binding domain of the transcription factor.
source: The number of base pairs that constitute the DNA 'footprint' within which base identity can influence binding affinity depends strongly on the three-dimensional structure of the DNA-binding domain (DBD) of the TF.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between protein structure and DNA binding.

claim: Under thermodynamic equilibrium, sequence specificity is completely defined by a table containing the relative affinity for each possible oligonucleotide within the footprint.
source: In theory, as long as thermodynamic equilibrium can be assumed, sequence specificity is completely defined by a table containing the (relative) affinity with which the DBD binds to each possible oligonucleotide within the footprint.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle based on thermodynamic equilibrium.

claim: The tabular approach has been widely used to analyze Protein Binding Microarray (PBM) data.
source: This tabular approach has been widely used to analyze Protein Binding Microarray (PBM) data (Berger and Bulyk, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Berger and Bulyk 2009.

claim: The size of the oligomer table grows exponentially with footprint size.
source: First, the size of the oligomer table grows exponentially with footprint size, which in practice limits it to eight base pairs, shorter than the footprint of most TFs.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the tabular approach.

claim: The tabular approach is in practice limited to eight base pairs.
source: First, the size of the oligomer table grows exponentially with footprint size, which in practice limits it to eight base pairs, shorter than the footprint of most TFs.
evidence: This is a practical limitation inferred from the exponential growth of parameters.

claim: Eight base pairs is shorter than the footprint of most transcription factors.
source: First, the size of the oligomer table grows exponentially with footprint size, which in practice limits it to eight base pairs, shorter than the footprint of most TFs.
evidence: This is a statement about typical TF footprint sizes.

claim: For octamer tables, the number of affinity parameters to be estimated is on the same order as the number of PBM data points.
source: Even for octamer tables, the number of affinity parameters to be estimated is on the same order as the number of PBM data points.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between parameters and data points in the tabular approach.

claim: The large number of parameters relative to data points limits precision in the tabular approach.
source: Even for octamer tables, the number of affinity parameters to be estimated is on the same order as the number of PBM data points. This limits precision and necessitates the use of non-parametric methods (as opposed to parameterized biophysical methods), resulting in an associated loss of quantitative information.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of having many parameters relative to data points.

claim: The large number of parameters necessitates the use of non-parametric methods in the tabular approach.
source: Even for octamer tables, the number of affinity parameters to be estimated is on the same order as the number of PBM data points. This limits precision and necessitates the use of non-parametric methods (as opposed to parameterized biophysical methods), resulting in an associated loss of quantitative information.
evidence: This is an inference about methodological requirements given the parameter-to-data ratio.

claim: Using non-parametric methods results in a loss of quantitative information.
source: Even for octamer tables, the number of affinity parameters to be estimated is on the same order as the number of PBM data points. This limits precision and necessitates the use of non-parametric methods (as opposed to parameterized biophysical methods), resulting in an associated loss of quantitative information.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of using non-parametric methods.

claim: An alternative to the tabular approach is to assume that each nucleotide position within the footprint contributes independently to overall binding affinity.
source: A long-standing alternative has been to assume that each nucleotide position within the footprint contributes independently to the overall binding affinity.
evidence: This describes an alternative modeling approach in the field.

claim: The position weight matrix (PWM) is the most commonly used representation of sequence specificity that makes the independence assumption.
source: The most commonly used representation of sequence specificity that makes this independence assumption is the position weight matrix (PWM) (Berg and von Hippel, 1987; Stormo and Fields, 1998; Stormo, 2000; Djordjevic et al., 2003), which defines position-specific base frequencies.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PWM algorithms traditionally aim to maximize information content relative to a random background model.
source: Algorithms for inferring the PWM coefficients traditionally aim to maximize its information content relative to a random background model (Lawrence et al., 1993; Frech et al., 1997; Bailey, 1995; Roth et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing PWM inference methods.

claim: Sequence specificity can be represented in terms of relative affinity associated with each possible point mutation of the optimal sequence.
source: In an alternative approach, sequence specificity is represented in terms of the relative affinity (or, equivalently, the difference, △△G, in binding free energy) associated with each possible point mutation of the optimal sequence (Stormo and Yoshioka, 1991; Stormo et al., 1993), and summarized in the form of a position-specific affinity matrix (PSAM) (Foat et al., 2006; Bussemaker et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing the PSAM approach.

claim: The difference in philosophy between PWM and PSAM representations leads to different approaches to estimating their coefficients.
source: The difference in philosophy between the PWM and PSAM representations also leads to a different approach to estimating their coefficients.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological consequences of different representations.

claim: In the PSAM approach, the ability to quantitatively explain variation in a measurable quantity is optimized rather than information content.
source: It is no longer the information content (i.e. the height of the letters in the standard sequence logo) that is being optimized, but rather the ability of the PSAM to quantitatively explain the variation in a measurable quantity in terms of variation in the nucleotide sequence associated with each quantity (for instance, the expression level of a gene in terms of its upstream promoter sequence).
evidence: This describes the optimization objective in the PSAM approach.

claim: For PBM data, PSAM parameters are inferred by performing a nonlinear fit of a sequence-based model that predicts signal intensity for each probe.
source: In the case of PBM data, the PSAM parameters are inferred by performing a nonlinear fit of a sequence-based model that predicts the signal intensity for each probe.
evidence: This describes the method for inferring PSAM parameters from PBM data.

claim: MatrixREDUCE was the first implementation of the PSAM approach for PBM data.
source: The first implementations of this idea were the MatrixREDUCE (Foat et al., 2006; Foat et al., 2005) and PREGO (Tanay, 2006) algorithms; a more recent extension is BEEML-PBM (Zhao and Stormo, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the original MatrixREDUCE papers.

claim: PREGO was one of the first implementations of the PSAM approach for PBM data.
source: The first implementations of this idea were the MatrixREDUCE (Foat et al., 2006; Foat et al., 2005) and PREGO (Tanay, 2006) algorithms; a more recent extension is BEEML-PBM (Zhao and Stormo, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the PREGO paper.

claim: BEEML-PBM is a more recent extension of the PSAM approach.
source: The first implementations of this idea were the MatrixREDUCE (Foat et al., 2006; Foat et al., 2005) and PREGO (Tanay, 2006) algorithms; a more recent extension is BEEML-PBM (Zhao and Stormo, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the BEEML-PBM paper.

claim: Whether dependencies between nucleotide positions can be accurately estimated from PBM data and used to refine binding specificity models remains an open question.
source: Whether dependencies between nucleotide positions can be accurately estimated from PBM data and used to refine models of binding specificity remains an open question (Weirauch, 2013; Zhao and Stormo, 2011; Benos et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations indicating ongoing debate in the field.

claim: The existence of alternative binding modes is now widely recognized.
source: Furthermore, while the existence of alternative binding modes is now widely recognized, accurate quantification of their relative usage has not yet been attempted.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Accurate quantification of relative usage of alternative binding modes has not yet been attempted.
source: Furthermore, while the existence of alternative binding modes is now widely recognized, accurate quantification of their relative usage has not yet been attempted.
evidence: This is a statement about what has not been done in the field prior to this work.

claim: FeatureREDUCE provides a flexible framework for building sequence-to-affinity models from PBM data.
source: To address these needs, we developed our FeatureREDUCE software. It provides a flexible framework for building sequence-to-affinity models from PBM data (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the purpose and capabilities of FeatureREDUCE, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: FeatureREDUCE uses a robust method to estimate relative affinities for each K-mer of a given length.
source: (1) A robust method is used to estimate relative affinities for each K-mer of a given length. The K-mer with the highest affinity is chosen as the seed.
evidence: This describes step 1 of the FeatureREDUCE algorithm as shown in Figure 1.

claim: FeatureREDUCE chooses the K-mer with the highest affinity as the seed.
source: (1) A robust method is used to estimate relative affinities for each K-mer of a given length. The K-mer with the highest affinity is chosen as the seed.
evidence: This describes the seed selection step in the FeatureREDUCE algorithm.

claim: FeatureREDUCE uses robust linear regression to estimate relative affinity parameters in each column of the PSAM.
source: (2) Using the seed as a reference, robust linear regression is used to estimate the relative affinity parameters in each column of the position-specific affinity matrix (PSAM).
evidence: This describes step 2 of the FeatureREDUCE algorithm.

claim: FeatureREDUCE uses linear regression to estimate the positional bias profile across the probe.
source: (3) With the current affinity model, linear regression is used to estimate the positional bias profile across the probe.
evidence: This describes step 3 of the FeatureREDUCE algorithm.

claim: FeatureREDUCE optionally uses nonlinear regression to solve for the free protein concentration.
source: (4) An optional step uses nonlinear regression to solve for the free protein concentration.
evidence: This describes an optional step 4 in the FeatureREDUCE algorithm.

claim: FeatureREDUCE uses robust regression to estimate free energy contributions associated with higher-order sequence features such as dinucleotides.
source: (5) Robust regression is used to estimate free energy contributions associated with higher-order sequence features such as dinucleotides.
evidence: This describes step 5 of the FeatureREDUCE algorithm.

claim: FeatureREDUCE repeats steps 2 through 5 until convergence.
source: (6) Steps 2 through 5 are repeated until convergence.
evidence: This describes the iterative nature of the FeatureREDUCE algorithm.

claim: FeatureREDUCE produces a feature-specific affinity model (FSAM) that can predict relative affinity for any DNA sequence.
source: (7) The procedure results in a feature-specific affinity model (FSAM) that can be used to predict the relative affinity for any DNA sequence.
evidence: This describes the output of the FeatureREDUCE algorithm.

claim: FeatureREDUCE is based on an extensible biophysical model where binding free energy difference is defined as a sum of parameters over all nucleotide sequence features.
source: FeatureREDUCE is based on an extensible biophysical model in which the binding free energy difference △△G(Sref→S) between an arbitrary nucleotide sequence S and a reference sequence Sref (usually taken as the highest-affinity sequence) is defined as a sum of parameters △△Gφ over all nucleotide sequence 'features' φ that distinguish S from Sref (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the theoretical foundation of FeatureREDUCE.

claim: The full set of possible features in FeatureREDUCE includes all possible single-base substitutions by default.
source: The full set of possible features in which S and Sref differ includes all possible single-base substitutions by default, but can be supplemented with dinucleotides that model dependencies and/or insertions at specific positions within the binding site that model variation in binding mode.
evidence: This describes the default feature set in FeatureREDUCE.

claim: FeatureREDUCE features can be supplemented with dinucleotides that model dependencies.
source: The full set of possible features in which S and Sref differ includes all possible single-base substitutions by default, but can be supplemented with dinucleotides that model dependencies and/or insertions at specific positions within the binding site that model variation in binding mode.
evidence: This describes an extension capability of FeatureREDUCE.

claim: FeatureREDUCE features can be supplemented with insertions at specific positions that model variation in binding mode.
source: The full set of possible features in which S and Sref differ includes all possible single-base substitutions by default, but can be supplemented with dinucleotides that model dependencies and/or insertions at specific positions within the binding site that model variation in binding mode.
evidence: This describes an extension capability of FeatureREDUCE for modeling multiple binding modes.

claim: A feature-based approach has been used previously for modeling protein-DNA binding.
source: Such a feature-based approach has been used previously (Sharon et al., 2008; Gordân et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2015), but, as we will argue below, our approach to estimating the coefficients of the model is different and optimal.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The FeatureREDUCE approach to estimating model coefficients is different from previous feature-based approaches.
source: Such a feature-based approach has been used previously (Sharon et al., 2008; Gordân et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2015), but, as we will argue below, our approach to estimating the coefficients of the model is different and optimal.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: The FeatureREDUCE approach to estimating model coefficients is optimal.
source: Such a feature-based approach has been used previously (Sharon et al., 2008; Gordân et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2015), but, as we will argue below, our approach to estimating the coefficients of the model is different and optimal.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by validation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The contribution of a binding site to PBM intensity depends on its position within the probe.
source: The contribution of a binding site to the PBM intensity depends on its position within the probe, as was previously demonstrated by planting the same motif at different offsets (Berger et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Berger et al. 2006.

claim: Positional dependence of binding site contribution may preclude accurate model estimation unless dealt with explicitly.
source: The contribution of a binding site to the PBM intensity depends on its position within the probe, as was previously demonstrated by planting the same motif at different offsets (Berger et al., 2006). This may preclude accurate model estimation unless it is dealt with explicitly.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of positional bias for model estimation.

claim: When a transcription factor binds near the free end of a probe, loss of contacts with the DNA backbone can reduce binding affinity.
source: Moreover, whenever the TF binds near the free end of a probe, loss of contacts with the DNA backbone can reduce binding affinity.
evidence: This is a biophysical explanation for reduced binding affinity at probe ends.

claim: FeatureREDUCE captures spatial bias by introducing an independent multiplicative correction factor for the ratio [TF]/Kd at each offset within the probe.
source: FeatureREDUCE captures such spatial bias by introducing an independent multiplicative correction factor for the ratio [TF]/Kd at each offset within the probe (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes how FeatureREDUCE models positional bias, with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The positional bias coefficients in FeatureREDUCE are estimated from PBM intensities in parallel with the △△G parameters.
source: FeatureREDUCE captures such spatial bias by introducing an independent multiplicative correction factor for the ratio [TF]/Kd at each offset within the probe (Figure 2a). These coefficients are estimated from the PBM intensities in parallel with the △△G parameters (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the parameter estimation procedure in FeatureREDUCE.

claim: The magnitude of the contribution of an individual Cbf1p binding site to PBM intensity can vary by an order of magnitude depending on its offset within the probe.
source: The positional bias profile inferred by FeatureREDUCE for the homo-dimer Cbf1p is shown in Figure 2b. It indicates that the magnitude of the contribution of an individual binding site to the PBM intensity can vary by an order of magnitude depending on its offset within the probe, and that there is preference for Cbf1p binding away from the substrate.
evidence: This is a finding from the positional bias analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Cbf1p has a preference for binding away from the substrate.
source: The positional bias profile inferred by FeatureREDUCE for the homo-dimer Cbf1p is shown in Figure 2b. It indicates that the magnitude of the contribution of an individual binding site to the PBM intensity can vary by an order of magnitude depending on its offset within the probe, and that there is preference for Cbf1p binding away from the substrate.
evidence: This is a finding from the positional bias analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Pho4p binding near the free end of the probe shows an opposite trend compared to Cbf1p.
source: For Pho4p, binding near the free end of the probe shows an opposite trend (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the positional bias analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fraction of variance in PBM intensity explained by a 10-bp independent-nucleotide model for Cbf1p increases from 48% to 71% after accounting for positional bias.
source: The fraction of the variance (R2) in PBM intensity explained by a 10-bp independent-nucleotide model increases dramatically, from 48% to 71%, after accounting for the positional bias.
evidence: This is a quantitative result demonstrating the importance of modeling positional bias.

claim: FeatureREDUCE can detect preference for monomeric transcription factors to bind in one of two possible orientations on dsDNA probes.
source: FeatureREDUCE can also detect any preference for monomeric TFs to bind in one of the two possible orientations on the dsDNA probes.
evidence: This describes a capability of FeatureREDUCE.

claim: Zif268 exhibits a strong bias for binding to the negative strand over the positive strand.
source: For example, Zif268 exhibits a strong bias for binding to the negative strand over the positive strand (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a finding from the orientation bias analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Zif268 requires non-specific contacts with the DNA backbone on the 5'-end of the motif.
source: Indeed, it is known that Zif268 requires non-specific contacts with the DNA backbone on the 5'-end of the motif (Berger et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Berger et al. 2006.

claim: BEEML-PBM models positional biases along the probes.
source: BEEML-PBM (Zhao and Stormo, 2011) also models positional biases along the probes, but it does not account for orientation preference, or for overhang binding at the free end of the probe.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of BEEML-PBM supported by a citation.

claim: BEEML-PBM does not account for orientation preference.
source: BEEML-PBM (Zhao and Stormo, 2011) also models positional biases along the probes, but it does not account for orientation preference, or for overhang binding at the free end of the probe.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of BEEML-PBM.

claim: BEEML-PBM does not account for overhang binding at the free end of the probe.
source: BEEML-PBM (Zhao and Stormo, 2011) also models positional biases along the probes, but it does not account for orientation preference, or for overhang binding at the free end of the probe.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of BEEML-PBM.

claim: The readout of base identity at different nucleotide positions is only approximately independent.
source: The readout of base identity at different nucleotide positions is only approximately independent.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of protein-DNA recognition.

claim: Various studies have analyzed whether representations of sequence specificity that account for nucleotide dependencies are more accurate than those that do not.
source: Indeed, various studies have analyzed whether representations of sequence specificity that account for nucleotide dependencies are more accurate than those that do not (Sharon et al., 2008; Agius et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2002; Stormo et al., 1986; Zhou and Liu, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Controversy remains about whether additional parameters associated with dependencies reflect structural mechanisms or technology-specific biases.
source: Controversy, however, remains about whether the additional parameters associated with such dependencies reflect structural mechanisms or technology-specific biases (Weirauch, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation indicating ongoing debate.

claim: In FeatureREDUCE, dependencies are modeled by including additional DNA sequence features that define base identity at two or more nucleotide positions.
source: In the biophysical model that underlies FeatureREDUCE, we model dependencies by simply including additional DNA sequence features φ that define base identity at two (or more) nucleotide positions, and estimating the corresponding free energy parameters △△Gφ along with those for single nucleotides (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes how FeatureREDUCE models nucleotide dependencies.

claim: Accounting for dependencies in the Cbf1p model significantly increased the fraction of variance explained when training on PBM intensities from 71% to 96%.
source: As expected for a model with additional parameters, accounting for dependencies significantly increased the fraction of the variance that could be explained when training on PBM intensities (R2 improved from 71% to 96%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting models to PBM data.

claim: Using robust regression is crucial for obtaining accurate estimates of contributions to binding free energy.
source: A unique aspect of FeatureREDUCE is the use of robust inference techniques (Huber and Ronchetti, 2009), which, as it turns out, is crucial for obtaining accurate estimates of the various contributions to the binding free energy.
evidence: This is a key finding about the importance of robust regression, supported by validation data.

claim: MITOMI measurements of Cbf1p binding affinity are in excellent agreement (R2 = 0.95) with surface plasmon resonance measurements.
source: To demonstrate this, we compared our results to measurements of binding affinity for Cbf1p obtained using the orginal version of the MITOMI technology (Maerkl and Quake, 2007), which are in excellent (R2 = 0.95) agreement with similar measurements obtained using surface plasmon resonance (Berger et al., 2006; Teh et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the relevant measurement papers.

claim: For Cbf1p PSAM model, RMSE between FeatureREDUCE predictions and MITOMI measurements improved from 0.071 to 0.035 when standard least-squares was replaced by robust regression.
source: When we fit a position-specific affinity matrix (PSAM) based model that ignores dependencies between nucleotides, the root-mean-square error (RMSE) between FeatureREDUCE model predictions and gold-standard MITOMI 1.0 measurements improved from 0.071 to 0.035 when standard least-squares fitting was replaced by robust iteratively re-weighted least-squares (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, left panels).
evidence: This is a quantitative validation result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: When using standard least-squares fitting, the FSAM model with dependencies performed worse than the PSAM model without dependencies for Cbf1p.
source: When positional dependencies were added to the model (feature-specific affinity model; FSAM), it actually performed worse than the model assuming independence between nucleotides (position-specific affinity matrix; PSAM) when we used standard least-squares fitting, indicative of over-fitting to noise in the training data.
evidence: This is a finding demonstrating over-fitting when not using robust regression.

claim: When using robust regression, the FSAM model for Cbf1p was significantly better than the PSAM model.
source: When we used robust regression, however, the RMSE for the FSAM-based model was significantly better than for the PSAM-based model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, right panels).
evidence: This is a quantitative validation result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dependencies within the binding interface exist and can be modeled correctly using robust regression.
source: These results indicate that dependencies within the binding interface indeed exist, and that they can be modeled incorrectly when non-robust regression techniques are used.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation results comparing robust and non-robust regression.

claim: Dependencies can be modeled incorrectly when non-robust regression techniques are used.
source: These results indicate that dependencies within the binding interface indeed exist, and that they can be modeled incorrectly when non-robust regression techniques are used.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation results.

claim: Including nucleotide dependencies when predicting yeast promoter affinities improves the ability to delineate Gene Ontology categories associated with Cbf1p regulation.
source: First, we found that the inclusion of nucleotide dependencies when predicting aggregated yeast promoter affinities improves the ability to delineate Gene Ontology categories associated with regulation by Cbf1p (see Materials and methods), but again only when robust inference techniques are used (Figure 3B; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The improvement in Gene Ontology delineation from including dependencies only occurs when robust inference techniques are used.
source: First, we found that the inclusion of nucleotide dependencies when predicting aggregated yeast promoter affinities improves the ability to delineate Gene Ontology categories associated with regulation by Cbf1p (see Materials and methods), but again only when robust inference techniques are used (Figure 3B; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: FeatureREDUCE performs well (RMSE = 0.075) at predicting in vivo Cbf1p occupancy at genomic E-box sites measured by ChIP-seq.
source: Using a simple thermodynamic equilibrium model with a single free protein concentration parameter to account for binding saturation in the ChIP-seq experiment, we found that by this in vivo measure, FeatureREDUCE performs well (RMSE = 0.075), and significantly better than BEEML-PBM (Zhao and Stormo, 2011) (RMSE = 0.156); full data are shown in Figure 4.
evidence: This is a quantitative validation result comparing predictions to ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: FeatureREDUCE performs significantly better than BEEML-PBM at predicting in vivo Cbf1p occupancy (RMSE = 0.075 vs 0.156).
source: Using a simple thermodynamic equilibrium model with a single free protein concentration parameter to account for binding saturation in the ChIP-seq experiment, we found that by this in vivo measure, FeatureREDUCE performs well (RMSE = 0.075), and significantly better than BEEML-PBM (Zhao and Stormo, 2011) (RMSE = 0.156); full data are shown in Figure 4.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between FeatureREDUCE and BEEML-PBM shown in Figure 4.

claim: FeatureREDUCE emerged as the top-performing algorithm in a benchmark comparison of 26 PBM data analysis algorithms according to both in vitro and in vivo metrics.
source: The accuracy of FeatureREDUCE was demonstrated more broadly in a recent benchmark comparison between 26 different PBM data analysis algorithms (Weirauch, 2013). This study employed two distinct performance metrics. The in vitro metric quantified the accuracy with which probe intensities were predicted in a test PBM experiment using a model trained on independent training data from a PBM experiment for the same TF but with a different probe design; this was done for 66 different TFs from various structural families. The in vivo metric used a non-parametric score to quantify accuracy in ranking sequences in terms of their local ChIP-seq enrichment, for nine different TFs. FeatureREDUCE emerged as the top-performing algorithm according to both criteria.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to the Weirauch 2013 benchmark study.

claim: Some algorithms generate models that perform well across different PBM designs but poorly when predicting in vivo binding.
source: However, one of their surprising findings was that some algorithms generate models that perform well across different PBM designs but poorly when predicting in vivo binding, presumably due to over-fitting to PBM-specific biases.
evidence: This is a finding from the Weirauch 2013 benchmark study.

claim: Poor in vivo prediction despite good PBM cross-validation is presumably due to over-fitting to PBM-specific biases.
source: However, one of their surprising findings was that some algorithms generate models that perform well across different PBM designs but poorly when predicting in vivo binding, presumably due to over-fitting to PBM-specific biases.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed discrepancy.

claim: FeatureREDUCE can perform forward selection of multiple binding modes represented by distinct PSAMs.
source: The modeling framework employed by FeatureREDUCE provides a natural opportunity to perform forward selection of multiple binding modes, represented by distinct PSAMs, which can subsequently be combined into a single predictive model and refined in an iterative manner (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a capability of FeatureREDUCE for modeling multiple binding modes.

claim: FeatureREDUCE accurately captures the known intrinsic half-site preference of Yap1p for TTAC.

claim: The FeatureREDUCE prediction of relative Gcn4p affinity is in good agreement with HiTS-FLIP measurements (Kd = 65 nM for TGACGTCA vs 15 nM for TGASTCA).

evidence: This is a validation of FeatureREDUCE predictions against independent measurements cited from Nutiu et al. 2011.

claim: The accuracy of the TGACGTCA motif for Gcn4p increases significantly (R2 from 69% to 80%) when using the multi-PSAM model compared to single-fit model for sites with relative affinity > 0.1.
source: In addition, while the accuracy of the dominant TGASTCA motif essentially does not change, the accuracy of the weaker TGACGTCA motif increases significantly when using our multi-PSAM model compared to the single-fit model (R2 improved from 69% to 80% for sites with relative affinity > 0.1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result demonstrating improved accuracy with the multi-PSAM model.

claim: The results of FeatureREDUCE multi-PSAM analysis can be used to predict which binding mode is dominant for a particular DNA sequence.

evidence: This describes a practical application of the multi-PSAM model.

claim: FeatureREDUCE analysis yields an accurate and interpretable biophysical affinity model.
source: In conclusion, FeatureREDUCE analysis yields an accurate and interpretable biophysical affinity model that can provide detailed clues about the structural mechanisms that underlie protein-DNA recognition (Roider et al., 2007; Kinney et al., 2007), such as dependencies between nucleotide positions and the modulation of binding mode by variation in the underlying DNA sequence.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the validation results presented in the manuscript.
